scan.summary: This is the company's own written emergency action plan for the Portland warehouse, lab and offices. It covers alarms, evacuation routes, the assembly point, headcount, shelter-in-place, first aid and training. Because the company wrote it, the company fixes it: update the text, fill the gaps listed below, and keep the maps and roster it refers to. It was last revised in February 2021 and nothing in the file shows a review since then.
scan.freshness_note: The last revision was February 2021, about five years and seven months ago. The plan says the facilities lead reviews it every January, which means reviews in January 2022 through January 2026 should exist, but none is recorded here. Ask for a newer version or for records of those reviews. If there are none, the plan needs a full review now: staffing, wardens, contractors, and the chemicals and layout may all have changed since 2021.

gaps.title: No procedure for reporting a fire or other emergency
gaps.description: The plan says pull stations are at each exit and that the alarm is monitored. It does not say who calls 911 or the fire department, how to report a chemical release or a medical emergency, or who notifies the monitoring company. Section 5 says EMS 'are called' but not by whom.
gaps.fix: Add a short 'Reporting an emergency' section: pull the nearest station and/or call 911 from a safe place, name who confirms the call with the monitoring company, and say how a spill or medical emergency is reported inside the building.
gaps.locator: not in the document (would sit between section 2 and section 3)
gaps.quote: Manual pull stations are located at each exit door.

gaps.title: Shutdown of critical equipment before evacuation is not set out
gaps.description: Section 3 tells employees to 'secure nothing that requires more than a few seconds'. It does not say which equipment, if any, is shut down before leaving (lab equipment, heaters, transfer pumps, forklift charging), who does it, or that nobody stays behind. The only shutdown step described is the ventilation shutdown during shelter-in-place.
gaps.fix: Either list the critical equipment, who shuts each piece down and when they leave, or state plainly that no one stays behind to shut down equipment and all staff leave at once.
gaps.quote: all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit.

gaps.title: No names or job titles of people to contact about the plan
gaps.description: The plan refers to a 'facilities lead', an 'incident coordinator' and a 'receptionist', but gives no names, and no contact person employees can go to for more information about the plan or their duties under it. Wardens and first-aid responders are said to be on a roster that is not in the file.
gaps.fix: Add a contacts block with the name or job title and phone number of the plan owner and the incident coordinator (plus a backup), and attach the current roster.
gaps.citation: OAR 437-002-0042(2)(f). I am relying on the earlier reading's paragraph letter; this search confirmed paragraphs (a) to (d) of the rule text.
gaps.quote: Any person unaccounted for is reported at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point

gaps.title: Plan does not say whether employees respond to chemical spills
gaps.description: This is a chemical distributor, and the plan covers 'chemical release'. It never says whether staff clean up or contain spills, or evacuate and leave it to an outside hazmat team. That choice decides whether the HAZWOPER emergency-response rules apply and what training is needed.
gaps.fix: State the spill policy. For example: incidental small spills are cleaned up by trained staff using the spill kit, and anything larger means evacuate and call 911 or hazmat. If employees respond beyond incidental spills, an emergency response plan and HAZWOPER training are needed.
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.120(q)(1) (belief, not checked against the Oregon adoption)
gaps.locator: not in the document (pages 2–3 mention chemical release only)
gaps.quote: what employees of Cascade Specialty Chemicals do when there is a fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency

gaps.title: Appendices A and B not in the file
gaps.description: The plan points to evacuation maps (Appendix A) and a floor warden and first-aid responder roster (Appendix B). Neither is in this file, so the exit routes, warden assignments and responder names cannot be checked.
gaps.fix: Attach the current maps and a dated roster to the plan, and confirm the posted copies match.
gaps.quote: Appendix B: Floor warden and first-aid responder roster (posted beside each evacuation map)

gaps.title: Annual January review not shown
gaps.description: The plan commits to a review every January. It still reads 'Revised February 2021' and has no review log, so there is no evidence of the reviews due in 2022 through 2026.
gaps.fix: Add a review log (date, reviewer, changes) and do a review now. Carry out the next one in January 2027.
gaps.quote: The facilities lead reviews the plan every January

gaps.title: Earthquake named in scope but no earthquake procedure
gaps.description: Section 1 lists earthquake as a covered emergency, but no section says what to do during or after one: drop, cover and hold on, staying clear of racking and chemical storage, when to evacuate, or checking for spills and gas leaks. This is a judgement based on the plan's own scope, not a specific rule paragraph I have checked.
gaps.fix: Add a short earthquake section: protective action during shaking, delayed evacuation once shaking stops, steering clear of racking, and checking for chemical releases before re-entry.
gaps.locator: page 2, section 1 (scope). The procedure is not in the document.
gaps.quote: fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency at the Portland facility

CASCADE SPECIALTY CHEMICALS, LLC
EMERGENCY ACTION PLAN
Portland Facility, 4410 NW Front Avenue, Portland, Oregon 97210
Revised February 2021
1. Purpose and scope
This Emergency Action Plan describes what employees of Cascade Specialty Chemicals do when there is
a fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency at the Portland facility. It
applies to all 42 employees at the Portland facility, including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office
staff, and to contractors and visitors while on site. The plan is kept in the front office and in the warehouse
break room, and a copy is available to any employee on request.
2. Alarm system
The building has a monitored fire alarm system with audible horns and strobe lights in the warehouse,
laboratory, loading dock and offices. The alarm is monitored 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety
under a service contract. Manual pull stations are located at each exit door. The alarm is tested on the first
Monday of each month by the facilities lead. A continuous horn means evacuate. Three short horns
repeated means shelter in place because of an outdoor hazard.
3. Evacuation procedures
When the continuous alarm sounds, all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a
few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit. Exit routes are posted on the evacuation maps at each
exit door and in Appendix A. Warehouse staff leave by the east dock doors or the north pedestrian door.
Laboratory staff leave by the laboratory's own exterior door on the south wall. Office staff leave by the
main entrance or the west stairwell. Do not use the freight lift. Do not return for belongings.
The assembly point is the far north end of the visitor parking lot, beside the flagpole, at least 150 feet
from the building. Employees assigned as floor wardens (one per area, listed on the warden roster posted
beside each evacuation map) sweep their area, close doors behind them, and report to the assembly point.
For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place
signal sounds. Employees move to the interior conference room or the laboratory corridor, close doors,
and the facilities lead shuts down the building ventilation from the mechanical room panel.
4. Accounting for employees after evacuation
At the assembly point each floor warden takes a headcount of the people from their area against the daily
sign-in sheet and the visitor log, which the receptionist brings out. Any person unaccounted for is reported
at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point, who passes the information to the fire
department on arrival. No one re-enters the building until the fire department or the incident coordinator
gives the all-clear. Evacuation drills are held twice a year, in spring and autumn.
5. Rescue and medical duties
Employees do not attempt rescue inside the building. First aid is given at the assembly point by the
trained first-aid responders (two per shift, named on the warden roster), who bring the first-aid kit and the
AED from the front office. An employee exposed to a chemical is taken to the emergency shower and
eyewash at the loading dock if it can be reached safely, or to the assembly point, and the SDS for the
product is brought to the responders. Emergency medical services are called for any injury beyond minor
first aid.
6. Training and review
Every new employee is walked through this plan, the exit routes for their work area and the assembly
point on their first day. Floor wardens and first-aid responders are trained annually. The plan is reviewed
with all employees whenever it is changed and whenever an employee's responsibilities under it change.
The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building
layout changes.
Appendix A: Evacuation maps (warehouse, laboratory, offices)
Appendix B: Floor warden and first-aid responder roster (posted beside each evacuation map)
